summary: Brick octagonal light at Port Sanilac on Lake Huron, first lit October 1886 with a fourth-order Fresnel lens; privately owned and closed to the public today.

lens.where: base of tower, in a plexiglass case

access.note: Privately owned; grounds, dwelling and tower closed (LighthouseFriends).

events.note: Tower, dwelling, privy and oil house completed 13 October 1886
Fixed white light shown from 20 October 1886 (Board notice; LighthouseFriends)
Sand Beach lifeboat capsized at Port Sanilac pier on 2 October 1888 while landing the St. Clair's people; five died
Ruby chimney placed on the lamp for a fixed red light (LighthouseFriends)
Oil to electric incandescent listed among the 1924 changes of illuminant (Lighthouse Service Bulletin 1924); LighthouseFriends also says the light was electrified in 1924
Fixed to flashing; oil to electric incandescent (Lighthouse Service Bulletin). LighthouseFriends dates the group-flash change to 1 April 1925.
Keeper's service ended with automation in 1928 (LighthouseFriends). The U.S. Lighthouse Society record gives 1925.
Dwelling sold to a private buyer (LighthouseFriends)
Tower sold to a private owner; the Coast Guard remains responsible for the light (LighthouseFriends)
Fresnel lens removed from the tower 13 September 2016; restored and placed in a case at the base of the tower
Group of three white flashes replaced by a white flash every 2.5 seconds, with a multi-tier LED beacon

keepers.name: Richard W. Morris
keepers.note: First head keeper. LighthouseFriends says he had been first assistant at Thunder Bay Island and reportedly resigned about the end of 1892; the archive roster ends his service in 1893.

keepers.name: William H. Holmes
keepers.note: Replaced Morris as first assistant at Thunder Bay Island in 1886 before coming to Port Sanilac (LighthouseFriends). Married Grace Sinclair, daughter of the Thunder Bay Island head keeper, in 1885. Died of apoplexy 13 October 1926, aged 64.

keepers.name: Grace Holmes
keepers.note: Wife of William H. Holmes; daughter and granddaughter of lighthouse keepers (LighthouseFriends). Appointed keeper in her husband's place; served until automation in 1928.

wrecks.outcome: Sand Beach life-boat capsized as it tried to beach at the Port Sanilac pier; five people died, among them the barge's captain and a woman cook. The St. Clair foundered.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The U.S. Lighthouse Society record gives automation in 1925; LighthouseFriends gives 1928 and says Grace Holmes kept the light until then. The electrification date also differs: the 1924 Lighthouse Service Bulletin lists Port Sanilac's oil-to-electric change among its 1924 changes, the 1925 Bulletin lists the flashing and electric change among its 1925 changes, and LighthouseFriends gives 1 April 1925 in one passage and 1924 in another. The story states the 1924 and 1925 Bulletin entries and both LighthouseFriends dates, and gives both automation dates.
LighthouseFriends says Morris reportedly resigned about the end of 1892; the archive roster gives service to 1893. The story reports both.

notes_for_editor: Most of the station history comes from LighthouseFriends, a copyrighted site: facts are restated in our own words, with one short quotation. Its family and personal details (Morris as Grace Holmes's uncle, the 1885 marriage, Grace's childhood, the Thunder Bay Island postings) rest on LighthouseFriends alone and should be checked against a primary record if one turns up. The Lighthouse Board reports for 1868 to 1890 are not in the local corpus (it holds Board reports for 1891 to 1901 only), so the $20,000 appropriation and the 1886 completion dates are not confirmed in an official report. NRHP nomination 84001842 is not digitised (the NPGallery PDF is a placeholder). The Northern Tribune (Cheboygan), 19 March 1885, p. 7, has an OCR-damaged item of '$10-000' for completing a lighthouse at or near Port Sanilac; this conflicts with the $20,000 figure and is not resolved. The Life-Saving Service's annual report for the fiscal year ending 30 June 1889 (the volume's title page; the volume's file name says 1888) gives the St. Clair account at printed pp. 21-23 (scan p. 29 is printed p. 21) and does not name the lighthouse; it is cited only for the wreck, which falls in fiscal 1889, not 1888. Private owners of the dwelling and tower are not named, by the guide's rule for converted lighthouses. The 1886 notice is OCR text, so its quotations are as printed, errors included.
